title: Osteoarthritis
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of Osteoarthritis
headings.content: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and is classified as a chronic, progressive, degenerative joint disease primarily affecting weight-bearing joints such as the hips, knees, and lumbar spine, as well as the hands. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding the pathophysiology of OA is essential for providing effective patient care. The disease process begins with the breakdown of articular cartilage, which normally acts as a smooth, shock-absorbing cushion between the bones. As cartilage degrades, it becomes frayed, pitted, and eventually wears away completely, leaving the underlying subchondral bone exposed. Without the protective cartilage layer, bone rubs against bone during movement, leading to friction, pain, inflammation, and stiffness. In response to this mechanical stress and microtrauma, the bone attempts to repair itself by forming abnormal bony outgrowths called osteophytes, or bone spurs, at the joint margins. Furthermore, mild synovial inflammation frequently develops due to the shedding of cartilage fragments into the joint space, triggering an immune response that causes joint effusion and swelling. Over time, these structural alterations lead to joint space narrowing, deformity, loss of range of motion, and significant functional impairment. The progressive nature of osteoarthritis means that nurses must be prepared to assess ongoing joint degeneration and implement interventions aimed at managing pain, preserving joint mobility, and enhancing the overall quality of life for affected clients.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: Understanding the etiology and risk factors associated with osteoarthritis is crucial for community health nursing and patient education. Osteoarthritis is broadly classified into two categories: primary (idiopathic) OA, which has no identifiable underlying systemic cause and is mostly related to the natural aging process, and secondary OA, which results from a specific predisposing event or condition. A primary risk factor for osteoarthritis is advanced age, as cumulative wear and tear over decades leads to structural fatigue of the cartilage matrix. Gender also plays a role; after the age of 50, women are significantly more likely than men to develop OA, particularly in the hands and knees, often linked to hormonal changes during menopause. Obesity is another major, modifiable risk factor, placing excessive mechanical load and stress on weight-bearing joints like the knees and hips, while systemic inflammatory mediators associated with adipose tissue may also contribute. Joint trauma, such as sports injuries, fractures involving the joint surface, or occupational injuries from repetitive bending and heavy lifting, can damage the cartilage and precipitate secondary OA later in life. Genetic predisposition, congenital joint abnormalities, and metabolic disorders can also weaken joint integrity. By identifying these risk factors, nursing students can effectively educate clients on weight management, injury prevention, and joint protection strategies to delay or minimize the onset of the disease.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of osteoarthritis develop insidiously and progress slowly over years. The hallmark symptom that prompts clients to seek medical attention is joint pain that typically worsens with physical activity and weight-bearing, and is notably relieved by rest. As the disease advances, pain may become persistent and present even at rest or during the night, disrupting sleep. Another classic symptom is joint stiffness, particularly in the morning or after periods of prolonged inactivity, though this morning stiffness is usually brief, lasting less than thirty minutes, which helps differentiate OA from inflammatory arthropathies like rheumatoid arthritis. Clients frequently report a sensation of joint crepitus—a grating, crackling, or popping sound and feeling during movement caused by bone ends rubbing together over irregular surfaces. Joint enlargement and bony swelling may be visibly apparent, especially in the hands where characteristic bony enlargements known as Heberden's nodes (at the distal interphalangeal joints) and Bouchard's nodes (at the proximal interphalangeal joints) develop. As joint stability decreases and muscle atrophy sets in from disuse, clients may experience a loss of range of motion, joint instability, muscle spasms, and altered gait. During assessment, nurses must thoroughly evaluate pain levels, functional limitations, joint symmetry, crepitus, and the impact of these symptoms on the client's activities of daily living.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation of osteoarthritis relies heavily on a thorough clinical history and physical examination, supported by imaging studies and laboratory tests to rule out other pathologies. Radiographic imaging, particularly standard plain X-rays, is the gold standard diagnostic tool for confirming OA. X-ray findings characteristic of osteoarthritis include joint space narrowing caused by the loss of cartilage, subchondral bone sclerosis (hardening of bone beneath the cartilage), the presence of osteophytes at the joint margins, and subchondral bone cysts. However, nurses should note that there is often a poor correlation between the severity of radiographic changes seen on an X-ray and the degree of pain or functional disability reported by the client. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is not routinely required for diagnosis, but it may be utilized when soft tissue structures such as menisci, ligaments, or early cartilage defects need visualization. Unlike systemic inflammatory joint diseases, routine laboratory blood tests such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and rheumatoid factor are typically normal in primary osteoarthritis. Joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) may be performed if joint effusion is significant or if infection or crystal-induced arthropathies like gout need to be ruled out; synovial fluid in OA is typically clear to pale yellow with normal to mild leukocyte counts, reflecting a non-inflammatory nature. These diagnostic tools help the healthcare team confirm the diagnosis and tailor an appropriate treatment plan.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of osteoarthritis aims to relieve pain, reduce joint inflammation, maintain or improve joint mobility, and minimize functional limitation, as there is currently no cure to reverse cartilage destruction. Management begins with non-pharmacological modalities, which serve as the foundation of therapy. These include weight reduction for overweight clients, regular low-impact aerobic exercise (such as swimming or walking) to strengthen supporting muscles, physical and occupational therapy, heat and cold applications, and the use of assistive devices like canes, walkers, or knee braces. Pharmacological management follows a stepped approach, starting with topical analgesics or oral medications. Acetaminophen is often considered a first-line oral analgesic for mild to moderate OA pain, though safety regarding liver function must be monitored. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or diclofenac, are widely used for their potent analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties, but nurses must educate clients about potential gastrointestinal ulceration, renal impairment, and cardiovascular risks. For clients with severe gastrointestinal risks, COX-2 selective inhibitors may be prescribed. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections can provide rapid, short-term relief during acute flare-ups of joint inflammation and effusion. Additionally, viscosupplementation involving intra-articular injections of hyaluronic acid derivatives may be used to restore joint lubrication. Nurses play a vital role in monitoring drug efficacy, assessing for adverse effects, and reinforcing adherence to the multi-modal treatment plan.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Rehabilitation
headings.content: Nursing care and rehabilitation are central to helping clients with osteoarthritis manage their chronic condition and maintain independence in daily activities. Nurses must conduct comprehensive baseline and ongoing assessments, focusing on pain severity, functional ability, joint mobility, skin integrity over pressure areas, and the client's psychological well-being. Pain management is a top nursing priority; nurses should administer prescribed analgesics timely, evaluate their effectiveness, and integrate non-pharmacological comfort measures such as applying warm compresses to relax stiff muscles and cold packs to reduce acute joint swelling. Exercise prescription is vital; nurses collaborate with physical therapists to encourage balanced regimens of rest and exercise, teaching clients to perform gentle range-of-motion exercises daily to prevent joint contractures and muscle atrophy. Clients should be guided to exercise during peak times of pain relief and to stop activities that cause sharp or prolonged joint pain. Occupational therapists assist clients in energy conservation techniques and the proper use of adaptive equipment, such as long-handled reachers, elevated toilet seats, and dressing aids, which reduce strain on affected joints. Furthermore, nurses provide psychosocial support, helping clients cope with chronic pain and lifestyle adaptations. Through continuous education and encouragement, nurses empower clients to actively participate in their rehabilitation and maintain an optimal quality of life.

headings.title: Surgical Interventions
headings.content: When conservative medical and rehabilitative measures fail to control severe pain, correct significant deformity, or restore functional ability, surgical interventions become necessary for clients with advanced osteoarthritis. Common surgical procedures include arthroscopic debridement and lavage, where loose cartilage fragments, osteophytes, and inflamed synovial tissue are removed from the joint cavity, often performed on knees to provide temporary relief. Osteotomy involves surgical cutting and realigning of the bone, either above or below the joint, to shift body weight away from the damaged, worn-out compartment of the joint to a healthier area; this is frequently used in younger, active clients with knee OA to delay the need for joint replacement. Arthrodesis, or joint fusion, permanently fuses the bones comprising the joint together, eliminating motion and thereby relieving pain; while highly effective for pain control, it results in loss of flexibility and is typically reserved for smaller joints such as the wrist or ankle. Total joint arthroplasty (joint replacement), involving the surgical removal of diseased joint surfaces and replacement with artificial metal, plastic, or ceramic prostheses, is the definitive surgical treatment for severe hip and knee osteoarthritis. Joint replacement dramatically reduces pain, corrects deformity, and restores functional independence. Perioperative nursing care for these clients involves rigorous pain management, deep breathing and coughing exercises, prevention of deep vein thrombosis through early ambulation and anticoagulants, careful neurovascular checks of the affected extremity, and structured physical therapy rehabilitation.

headings.title: Complications and Client Education
headings.content: Complications and comprehensive client education are essential components of nursing management for individuals living with osteoarthritis. Chronic pain, joint instability, and muscle weakness can lead to severe physical deconditioning, an increased risk of falls, and loss of independence in performing activities of daily living. Furthermore, chronic reliance on pharmacological agents like NSAIDs can lead to systemic complications such as peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal failure, and cardiovascular events. Client education must empower individuals to take an active role in self-management to prevent these complications. Nurses should educate clients on weight management strategies, proper body mechanics, and joint protection techniques, such as distributing weight across multiple joints, avoiding prolonged standing or repetitive squatting, and using ergonomic tools. Clients must be instructed on the safe and correct use of assistive devices like canes (which should be held in the hand opposite the affected joint) and walkers. Education should also cover medication safety, emphasizing adherence to prescribed dosages, recognizing adverse drug reactions, and avoiding unverified herbal remedies that may interact with prescribed drugs. Additionally, nurses should encourage ongoing communication with healthcare providers, adherence to scheduled physical therapy regimens, and participation in community support groups. By providing clear, compassionate education, nurses help clients navigate the challenges of osteoarthritis and maintain a high quality of life.
